newsitem.title: HUNGARY: OECD cautious on Hungary's improving economy.
newsitem.headline: OECD cautious on Hungary's improving economy.

text.p: Hungary's economy is moving out of recession, with output, domestic demand and investment strengthening but inflation remains high, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Thursday.

"Output growth is now strengthening and demand is becoming more balanced with investment picking up strongly," the OECD said in an economic outlook, adding that overall GDP growth could be around 2.5 percent this year and 3.5 percent in 1998, following a figure of under one percent for 1996.

"There were increasing signs towards the end of 1996 of a return to faster growth. Recent data indicate an acceleration of private sector manufacturing investment and export sales. Business confidence is strengthening," the report said.

Hungary has been subject to a strict austerity programme since March 1995 in order to rein in soaring current account and budget deficits. The measures have resulted in mininal growth and a 17 percent fall in real wages.
However while both deficits have been reduced significantly the social security deficit was still too high while tax evasion was preventing further reductions.

"While there has been a substantial improvement in the government balance, a deficit in the social security funds and poor tax compliance have prevented faster progress in bringing government revenues and expenditures into balance.
Hungary's government said on Thursday the social security deficit was likely to overshoot the 13.5 billion forint target for 1997 by some 20 billion forints.

A further problem was that inflation may not come down as quickly as the five percent per year hoped for by the government, with the crawling peg devaluation of the forint, currently 1.1 percent per month, only helping partly in keeping inflation in check.
"The (crawling peg) policy has effectively maintained the real exchange rate constant while keeping real interest rates low," the report said.
"(But) despite a significant fall (from 28 percent in December 1995 to 18 percent now), the implicit inflation target of 17 to 18 percent for the year implies only moderate disinflation."
The report added that unless a package is agreed with unions and employers which combines an incomes policy with a slower rate of crawl, inflation is unlikely to fall below 15 percent in 1998.
The report predicted unemployment would remain at around 10 percent despite further job losses because the workforce was shrinking.
"Continued restructuring will translate into further employment losses and labour force contraction but by 1998 emnployment should have stopped falling," it said.
The report said private consumption would recover but was unlikely to grow by more than one percent a year over the next two years unless there is an unanticipated fall in the saving ratio.

It concluded that apart from inflation the main areas of uncertainty relate to the strength of the recoveries in domestic demand and imports, with implications for government revenues and the current account deficit.

"A widening of the current account deficit may not create serious difficulties if export growth remains robust since a substantial part of it is likely to be financed through direct foreign investment rather than debt-creating inflows," the report said.
